title: What Is Going on with AI in K-12 Anyway?
author: Nick Potkalitsky
summary: Nick Potkalitsky reports from the EduCon conference with a state-of-play survey of K-12 AI adoption in early 2024. He opens by noting that presenters meant very different things by human-centric AI, then describes where public schools, private schools and a few pioneering educators actually stand. Public districts are largely stalled by bans and distrust of model makers over student data, while private schools lack policies and have seen essay-drafting experiments fail for all but advanced writers. He then offers three recommendations, security, infrastructure and pedagogy, and closes with five proposed student-level AI learning outcomes. The piece is a practitioner's conference synthesis rather than research, but it captures the early-2024 concerns of school technology teams concretely.
points: Public schools in the New York, Philadelphia and DC areas had progressed very little, constrained by top-down AI bans and distrust of vendors with student data.
Private-school experiments with having students edit AI-drafted essays were dropped because only stronger writers could evaluate the output.
Potkalitsky argues that credible data-security commitments from providers are the precondition for any K-12 AI progress.
Infrastructure and licensing costs are real, with a rough figure of at least ten thousand dollars for a secure GPT-4-class product in a school of about 1,000 students.
He proposes five student AI learning outcomes that pair AI literacy and ethics with continued mastery of traditional writing skills.
quotes: For one presenter, it meant students relying on AI for up to 50% of text generation while maintaining their ideas and authentic voice. For another, "human-centric" meant that teachers should never use AI to write lesson plans or assignment prompts.

This team’s hesitancy is two-fold. Externally, their district presently has a top-down ban on all AI tools across school computer networks as decided by the superintendent in consultation with the school board.

Initially, some educators experimented with having students use AI to draft essays for further development, but this approach was quickly abandoned. It turned out that only students with more advanced abilities could effectively evaluate AI-generated content to create new insights and improve their writing.

My investigations revealed that obtaining these accounts can be quite tricky. Currently, these licenses are only sold in batches of 300 or more, presenting a challenge for smaller organizations or those not fully integrated with Microsoft products.
Without firm commitments from AI providers regarding the protection of their products, progress in integrating AI into K-12 education will remain stagnant. Period.

During a recent workshop I participated in, experts unequivocally stated that the free version of ChatGPT-3.5 falls short for academic use due to its limited capacity in generating thoughtful, Socratic responses to well-designed prompts. In essence, while GPT-3.5 is adept at providing answers, it struggles with explaining them, thereby diminishing its utility as an educational resource.

Teachers, administrators, technology directors, parents, and students need to work collaboratively to develop pedagogy and curriculum best suited to the environments and purposes of particular school communities, grade levels, and pre-professional programs. While organizations like AAAA, CSTA, and ITSE are hard at work developing standards to guide integration and implementation of AI in today’s classrooms, schools and district ultimately need to determine their own purposes and outcomes for AI integration and development.
